label: Lab notebook: the problem

diff.text: Drone arm vibrates at ~180 Hz while hovering. Camera footage is blurry.
Idea: fill the arm with a 3D-printed lattice to absorb the vibration.
Papers: lattices work well in simulation; few have been tested on real drones.

why: The camera footage was unusable. That practical problem is where the research question came from.

content.summary: Reading papers on vibration-damping lattice structures and taking notes.

messages.text: Plan: simulate 3 lattice designs, print the best one, test it on the shaker table.
Good. Simulate first so you don't waste printer time.

content.prompt: Help me set up a simulation over 3 lattice cell sizes and report the first resonance frequency of each.

steps.summary: Help me set up a simulation over 3 lattice cell sizes and report the first resonance frequency of each.
Done. Predicted first resonance: 212 Hz (2 mm cells), 236 Hz (3 mm), 251 Hz (4 mm). The 3 mm design gives the best balance of stiffness and weight.

commits.message: Add simulation sweep over lattice cell size
Export predicted frequencies to a table

diff.text: Printed the 3 mm lattice arm and mounted it on the shaker table.
Measured first resonance: 164 Hz. Simulation predicted 236 Hz.
That's 30% off. Rechecked the mounting; that isn't the cause.

label: Simulation and test disagree

messages.text: Test shows 164 Hz, simulation said 236 Hz. 30% off and I can't find the bug.
It may not be a bug. Printed plastic is often softer than the datasheet says. Measure it yourself.

why: I spent a week sure I had a coding error. It never occurred to me that the material itself was the problem.
turning_point: Simulation and experiment disagree by 30%. The whole plan assumed the simulation was right, and now that assumption is in doubt.

content.summary: Plotting the measured vibration spectrum against the simulation's prediction.

label: Rewrote the test plan

diff.text: Material stiffness: measure it with pull tests on printed bars.
Next: re-run the simulation with the measured stiffness.

why: Measuring the material cost three extra weeks. But without it, every design would be built on a wrong number.

messages.text: Print bars in two directions. Printed parts are usually stiffer along the layers than across them.

content.prompt: I have force and stretch data from 10 pull tests in a spreadsheet. Help me calculate each bar's stiffness and compare the two print directions.

steps.summary: I have force and stretch data from 10 pull tests in a spreadsheet. Help me calculate each bar's stiffness and compare the two print directions.
Along the layers: 2.6 GPa on average. Across the layers: 1.9 GPa. Both are well below the 3.5 GPa datasheet value, which explains most of the 30% gap.

commits.message: Use measured stiffness in the simulation

content.summary: Re-running the simulation with the measured stiffness and checking it against the test.

label: Simulation now matches

messages.text: New simulation: 169 Hz. Test: 164 Hz. Within 3%!
That correction is the real contribution. Others simulating printed parts have the same problem. Make that the paper.

why: My advisor reframed the project in one message. I'd been treating the material problem as a detour, but it was the most useful result.
turning_point: The fix becomes the finding. The paper shifts from "a better damper" to "how to simulate 3D-printed parts accurately."

content.prompt: Re-run the simulation for all three cell sizes with the measured stiffness, and make a chart of predicted vs. measured frequency.

steps.summary: Re-run the simulation for all three cell sizes with the measured stiffness, and make a chart of predicted vs. measured frequency.
Updated predictions are within 2–4% of the tests for all three designs. Chart saved as Figure 3.

commits.message: Re-run all designs with measured stiffness

diff.text: Printed parts were 26–46% less stiff than the datasheet value.
Using the measured stiffness cut the prediction error from 30% to under 4% (Figure 3).

label: Changed the title

diff.text: A 3D-Printed Lattice Damper for Drone Arms
Why Simulations of 3D-Printed Lattices Miss, and How to Fix It

why: Changing the title felt like admitting the original idea had failed. But this is the result people will actually use.

messages.text: Figure 3 is great. Add error bars from the 10 pull tests.
Adding them, then sending to my advisor Friday.

diff.text: Reviewer 2: Does the correction hold for other printers or plastics?
Plan: test a second plastic on a different printer.

content.prompt: A reviewer asks whether this works for other plastics. Help me plan the smallest test that would answer that.

steps.summary: A reviewer asks whether this works for other plastics. Help me plan the smallest test that would answer that.

Print 5 bars and one lattice arm in a second plastic (PETG) on a different printer. If the corrected simulation still lands within 5% of the test, that supports the method without redoing the whole study.

label: Added second-material test

diff.text: With PETG on a second printer, corrected predictions were within 5% of the tests.

why: The reviewer pushed me to test something I'd been avoiding. It made the paper much stronger.
